claim: TRIM33 is a lineage dependency in B cell neoplasms.
source: TRIM33 is identified here as a lineage dependency in B cell neoplasms
evidence: Supported by RNAi screen data showing selective requirement in B-ALL cells and validation in multiple B cell lines

claim: TRIM33 performs its essential function in B cell neoplasms by associating with a single cis element.
source: TRIM33 is identified here as a lineage dependency in B cell neoplasms and is shown to perform this essential function by associating with a single cis element.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing preferential TRIM33 binding and CRISPR deletion experiments demonstrating that deletion of the Bim -117 enhancer renders TRIM33 dispensable

claim: ChIP-seq analysis of TRIM33 in murine B cell leukemia revealed a preferential association with two lineage-specific enhancers.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of TRIM33 in murine B cell leukemia revealed a preferential association with two lineage-specific enhancers that harbor an exceptional density of motifs recognized by the PU.1 TF.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq experimental data showing TRIM33 enrichment at Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions

claim: The two strongest sites of TRIM33 enrichment harbor an exceptional density of motifs recognized by the PU.1 transcription factor.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of TRIM33 in murine B cell leukemia revealed a preferential association with two lineage-specific enhancers that harbor an exceptional density of motifs recognized by the PU.1 TF.
evidence: Supported by FIMO motif analysis showing 17 PU.1 motif instances at Bim -117 and 14 instances at Atp1b3 -35

claim: TRIM33 is recruited to PU.1/TRIM33 co-occupied enhancers by PU.1.
source: TRIM33 is recruited to these elements by PU.1, yet acts to antagonize PU.1 function.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing that PU.1 knockdown leads to loss of TRIM33 occupancy at these sites

claim: TRIM33 acts to antagonize PU.1 function at co-occupied enhancers.
source: TRIM33 is recruited to these elements by PU.1, yet acts to antagonize PU.1 function.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRIM33 knockdown increases PU.1 occupancy and H3K27 acetylation at Bim -117

claim: One of the PU.1/TRIM33 co-occupied enhancers is upstream of the pro-apoptotic gene Bim.
source: One of the PU.1/TRIM33 co-occupied enhancers is upstream of the pro-apoptotic gene Bim, and deleting this enhancer renders TRIM33 dispensable for leukemia cell survival.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing TRIM33 and PU.1 occupancy at a region 117 kb upstream of Bim

claim: Deleting the Bim -117 enhancer renders TRIM33 dispensable for leukemia cell survival.
source: One of the PU.1/TRIM33 co-occupied enhancers is upstream of the pro-apoptotic gene Bim, and deleting this enhancer renders TRIM33 dispensable for leukemia cell survival.
evidence: Supported by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion experiments showing B-ALL cells with homozygous deletion of Bim -117 do not require TRIM33 for viability

claim: TRIM33 prevents apoptosis in B lymphoblastic leukemia by interfering with enhancer-mediated Bim activation.
source: These findings reveal an essential role for TRIM33 in preventing apoptosis in B lymphoblastic leukemia by interfering with enhancer-mediated Bim activation.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRIM33 knockdown leads to Bim upregulation and apoptosis, and that Bim knockdown rescues TRIM33 loss

claim: DNA-binding transcription factors typically recognize short 6–12 base-pair motifs.
source: DNA-binding transcription factors (TFs) typically recognize short 6–12 base-pair motifs, which exist at a high frequency in mammalian genomes (Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009; Spitz and Furlong, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Short TF recognition motifs exist at a high frequency in mammalian genomes.
source: DNA-binding transcription factors (TFs) typically recognize short 6–12 base-pair motifs, which exist at a high frequency in mammalian genomes (Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009; Spitz and Furlong, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Transcription factors occupy thousands of genomic sites in any given cell type.
source: While chromatin restricts the accessibility of these sequences, TFs nonetheless occupy thousands of genomic sites in any given cell type (Spitz and Furlong, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature and specific examples provided

claim: MyoD has been detected at approximately 39,000 sites in primary myotubes.
source: As examples, MyoD has been detected at ∼39,000 sites in primary myotubes and Pax5 at ∼20,000 sites in B cell progenitors (Cao et al., 2010; Revilla et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Pax5 has been detected at approximately 20,000 sites in B cell progenitors.
source: As examples, MyoD has been detected at ∼39,000 sites in primary myotubes and Pax5 at ∼20,000 sites in B cell progenitors (Cao et al., 2010; Revilla et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Transcriptional cofactors are known to occupy the mammalian genome in a generalized manner.
source: Furthermore, transcriptional cofactors (coactivators and corepressors) are also known to occupy the mammalian genome in a generalized manner (Ram et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In prokaryotic species, transcription factors can occupy as few as one or two sites in an entire genome to implement precise transcriptional responses.
source: This is in stark contrast to prokaryotic species, in which TFs can occupy as few as one or two sites in an entire genome to implement precise transcriptional responses (Martínez-Antonio and Collado-Vides, 2003; Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRIM33 belongs to the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein family of E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: TRIM33, also known as TIF1γ, belongs to the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein family of E3 ubiquitin ligases (Venturini et al., 1999; Hatakeyama, 2011; Herquel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRIM33 and its homologs TRIM24 and TRIM28 belong to a subfamily of ubiquitously expressed TRIM proteins that contain a tandem plant homeodomain (PHD) and bromodomain module.
source: TRIM33 and its homologs TRIM24 and TRIM28 belong to a subfamily of ubiquitously expressed TRIM proteins that contain a tandem plant homeodomain (PHD) and bromodomain module and function as transcriptional cofactors (Venturini et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: TRIM33, TRIM24, and TRIM28 function as transcriptional cofactors.
source: TRIM33 and its homologs TRIM24 and TRIM28 belong to a subfamily of ubiquitously expressed TRIM proteins that contain a tandem plant homeodomain (PHD) and bromodomain module and function as transcriptional cofactors (Venturini et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: TRIM33 has a role in the TGFβ signaling pathway through regulation of SMAD4 mono-ubiquitination.
source: One role of TRIM33 is in the TGFβ signaling pathway, which occurs through regulation of SMAD4 mono-ubiquitination and/or by functioning as a cofactor for the TFs SMAD2 and SMAD3 (Dupont et al., 2005, 2009; He et al., 2006; Agricola et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRIM33 functions as a cofactor for the transcription factors SMAD2 and SMAD3.
source: One role of TRIM33 is in the TGFβ signaling pathway, which occurs through regulation of SMAD4 mono-ubiquitination and/or by functioning as a cofactor for the TFs SMAD2 and SMAD3 (Dupont et al., 2005, 2009; He et al., 2006; Agricola et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRIM33 interacts with the transcription factor SCL/TAL1 to promote transcription elongation of erythroid-specific genes.
source: TRIM33 is also known to interact with the TF SCL/TAL1 to promote transcription elongation of erythroid-specific genes, which may occur through the recruitment of FACT and P-TEFb complexes (Bai et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRIM33 can form repressive complexes with SCL to block transcriptional activation.
source: However, another study suggests that TRIM33 can form repressive complexes with SCL to block transcriptional activation (Kusy et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The PHD-bromodomain module of TRIM33 interacts with covalently modified histone tails.
source: The PHD-bromodomain module of TRIM33 interacts with covalently modified histone tails, which can further stabilize TRIM33 chromatin occupancy and stimulate its E3 ligase activity (Tsai et al., 2010; Agricola et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Interaction of TRIM33's PHD-bromodomain module with modified histone tails can stabilize TRIM33 chromatin occupancy and stimulate its E3 ligase activity.
source: The PHD-bromodomain module of TRIM33 interacts with covalently modified histone tails, which can further stabilize TRIM33 chromatin occupancy and stimulate its E3 ligase activity (Tsai et al., 2010; Agricola et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A negative selection RNAi screen in B-ALL cells identified 16 chromatin regulator dependencies.
source: 1,126 shRNAs targeting 259 chromatin regulators were assessed individually for effects on the viability of B-ALL cells in culture, which led to the identification of 16 dependencies after applying stringent scoring criteria (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental screen data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The majority of chromatin regulator dependencies identified in B-ALL had been identified in a prior screen in MLL-AF9/NrasG12D acute myeloid leukemia.
source: The majority of these factors had been identified in a prior screen that evaluated the requirement of chromatin regulators in MLL-AF9/NrasG12D acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (Zuber et al., 2011b), however TRIM33 was identified here as a unique requirement in B-ALL.
evidence: Supported by comparison with published screen data

claim: TRIM33 was identified as a unique requirement in B-ALL compared to AML.
source: The majority of these factors had been identified in a prior screen that evaluated the requirement of chromatin regulators in MLL-AF9/NrasG12D acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (Zuber et al., 2011b), however TRIM33 was identified here as a unique requirement in B-ALL.
evidence: Supported by comparison of screen results between B-ALL and AML

claim: The six TRIM33 shRNAs used in the screen exhibited a close correlation between knockdown efficiency and loss of B-ALL viability.
source: The six TRIM33 shRNAs used in the screen exhibited a close correlation between knockdown efficiency and loss of B-ALL viability, suggesting on-target effects (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: A v-Abl transformed B cell progenitor line (38B9) is sensitive to TRIM33 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, a v-Abl transformed B cell progenitor line, 38B9 (Alt et al., 1984), and several human B cell cancer lines were also sensitive to TRIM33 knockdown (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Several human B cell cancer lines are sensitive to TRIM33 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, a v-Abl transformed B cell progenitor line, 38B9 (Alt et al., 1984), and several human B cell cancer lines were also sensitive to TRIM33 knockdown (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the viability of MLL-AF9/NrasG12D AML.
source: In contrast, TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the viability of MLL-AF9/NrasG12D AML and Notch-mutant T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the viability of Notch-mutant T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).
source: In contrast, TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the viability of MLL-AF9/NrasG12D AML and Notch-mutant T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Upon knockdown of TRIM33, B-ALL cells underwent apoptosis.
source: Upon knockdown of TRIM33, B-ALL cells underwent apoptosis, as shown by Annexin V/DAPI staining (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V/DAPI staining data shown in Figure 1F

claim: TRIM33 is essential for the survival of neoplastic B cells.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that TRIM33 is essential for the survival of neoplastic B cells.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including viability assays and apoptosis measurements

claim: Doxycycline-regulated shRNA transgenic mice exhibited dox-dependent suppression of TRIM33 in multiple tissues.
source: When crossed with mice that express rtTA-M2 from the ROSA26 promoter, animals exhibited dox-dependent suppression of TRIM33 in multiple tissues (Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of bone marrow and spleen following 1 or 4 weeks of dox administration revealed a selective loss of CD19+ and B220+ B lymphoid cells in TRIM33-deficient animals.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of the bone marrow and spleen following 1 or 4 weeks of dox administration revealed a selective loss of CD19+ and B220+ B lymphoid cells in TRIM33-deficient animals, while erythroid, myeloid, and T lymphoid populations remained intact or even increased in relative abundance (Figures 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1I and 1J

claim: Erythroid, myeloid, and T lymphoid populations remained intact or increased in relative abundance in TRIM33-deficient animals.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of the bone marrow and spleen following 1 or 4 weeks of dox administration revealed a selective loss of CD19+ and B220+ B lymphoid cells in TRIM33-deficient animals, while erythroid, myeloid, and T lymphoid populations remained intact or even increased in relative abundance (Figures 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1I and 1J

claim: B cell production recovered fully in TRIM33-deficient mice upon restoring TRIM33 expression.
source: Taking advantage of the reversibility of the dox-regulated shRNA system, we found that B cell production recovered fully in TRIM33-deficient mice upon restoring TRIM33 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the histological appearance of colon, liver, thymus, and pancreatic tissues.
source: Notably, TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the histological appearance of colon, liver, thymus, and pancreatic tissues and led to no significant changes in animal weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: TRIM33 knockdown led to no significant changes in animal weight.
source: Notably, TRIM33 knockdown led to negligible effects on the histological appearance of colon, liver, thymus, and pancreatic tissues and led to no significant changes in animal weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by weight measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: B lymphoid cells are uniquely sensitive to TRIM33 inhibition.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that B lymphoid cells are uniquely sensitive to TRIM33 inhibition, thus implicating TRIM33 as a lineage dependency in cancers of B cell origin.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations in transgenic mice and cell lines

claim: Trim33−/− mice exhibit a B lymphocyte deficiency and an expansion of myeloid cells.
source: These results are in agreement with the prior characterization of Trim33−/− mice, which were found to exhibit a B lymphocyte deficiency and an expansion of myeloid cells (Aucagne et al., 2011; Kusy et al., 2011; Bai et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Bim and Atp1b3 were the two most upregulated genes upon TRIM33 depletion in B-ALL cells.
source: This analysis revealed a distribution of gene expression changes, however, we noted that Bim and Atp1b3 were the two most upregulated genes upon TRIM33 depletion (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The two strongest sites of TRIM33 enrichment in B-ALL were located 117 kb upstream of Bim and 35 kb upstream of Atp1b3.
source: Remarkably, the two strongest sites of TRIM33 enrichment in B-ALL were located 117 kb upstream of Bim (in an intron of a non-expressed gene Acoxl) and at a site 35 kb upstream of Atp1b (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 2B-D

claim: The TRIM33-occupied regions upstream of Bim and Atp1b3 were enriched for H3K27 acetylation but not for H3K4 tri-methylation, suggesting that these elements are active enhancers.
source: The TRIM33-occupied regions upstream of Bim and Atp1b3 were enriched for H3K27 acetylation but not for H3K4 tri-methylation, suggesting that these elements are active enhancers (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data for histone modifications shown in Figures 2C and 2D, and citation to published literature on enhancer marks

claim: TRIM33 occupancy was observed at the Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions in 38B9, AML, and whole spleen, but not in T-ALL.
source: We also observed TRIM33 occupancy at these same two regions in 38B9, AML, and in whole spleen, but not in T-ALL (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: TRIM33 exhibits a strong bias for a small number of genomic locations in B-ALL.
source: A striking attribute of the genomewide pattern of TRIM33 occupancy was its strong bias for a small number of locations, with lower levels of enrichment at other sites across the genome (Figure 2E,F, and Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 2E, 2F, and supplementary figures

claim: The Bim -117 region possesses 17 instances of sequence motifs recognized by PU.1.
source: Using the FIMO motif analysis tool (Grant et al., 2011), we found that both of these regions possessed a high density of sequence motifs recognized by PU.1 (17 instances at Bim –117 and 14 instances at Atp1b3 –35), which is an essential hematopoietic TF expressed in B lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Scott et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by FIMO motif analysis

claim: The Atp1b3 -35 region possesses 14 instances of sequence motifs recognized by PU.1.
source: Using the FIMO motif analysis tool (Grant et al., 2011), we found that both of these regions possessed a high density of sequence motifs recognized by PU.1 (17 instances at Bim –117 and 14 instances at Atp1b3 –35), which is an essential hematopoietic TF expressed in B lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Scott et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by FIMO motif analysis

claim: PU.1 is an essential hematopoietic transcription factor expressed in B lymphoid and myeloid lineages.
source: Using the FIMO motif analysis tool (Grant et al., 2011), we found that both of these regions possessed a high density of sequence motifs recognized by PU.1 (17 instances at Bim –117 and 14 instances at Atp1b3 –35), which is an essential hematopoietic TF expressed in B lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Scott et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A much lower density of motifs for E2A, EBF1, or PAX5 was observed at the Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions compared to PU.1 motifs.
source: In contrast, we observed a much lower density of motifs for other TFs involved in B cell specific transcriptional regulation (E2A, EBF1, or PAX5) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis data shown in Figures 3A and 3B

claim: TRIM33 has been shown previously to interact with PU.1.
source: Since TRIM33 has been shown previously to interact with PU.1 (Kusy et al., 2011), we investigated whether PU.1 promotes TRIM33 recruitment to these regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: ChIP-seq analysis of PU.1 in B-ALL confirmed its association with Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of PU.1 in B-ALL confirmed its association with Bim –117 and Atp1b3 –35, as well as with more than 2600 other genomic sites (Figure 2C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: PU.1 associates with more than 2600 genomic sites in B-ALL.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of PU.1 in B-ALL confirmed its association with Bim –117 and Atp1b3 –35, as well as with more than 2600 other genomic sites (Figure 2C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions are outliers when compared to other PU.1-occupied sites with regard to the overall density of PU.1 recognition motifs.
source: Remarkably, Bim –117 and Atp1b3 –35 regions are outliers when compared to other PU.1-occupied sites with regard to the overall density of PU.1 recognition motifs and the overall level of PU.1 enrichment (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions are outliers when compared to other PU.1-occupied sites with regard to the overall level of PU.1 enrichment.
source: Remarkably, Bim –117 and Atp1b3 –35 regions are outliers when compared to other PU.1-occupied sites with regard to the overall density of PU.1 recognition motifs and the overall level of PU.1 enrichment (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The level of H3K27ac at Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 is not skewed towards these two locations, indicating that these regions are not super-enhancers.
source: The level of the active enhancer chromatin mark, H3K27ac, is not skewed in a similar manner towards these two locations, indicating that these regions are not super-enhancers that exhibit high levels of all regulators (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to super-enhancer literature

claim: PU.1 occupancy was confirmed at the Bim -117 and Atp1b3 -35 regions in 38B9 and AML cells, but not in T-ALL.
source: Using ChIP-qPCR, we also confirmed PU.1 occupancy at these two regions in 38B9 and AML cells, but not in T-ALL (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: PU.1 knockdown led to a significant loss of TRIM33 occupancy at Bim and Atp1b3 in proportion to the loss of PU.1.
source: We found that PU.1 knockdown led to a significant loss of TRIM33 occupancy at Bim and Atp1b3 in proportion to the loss of PU.1 (Figure 3D,E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 3D, 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells displayed normal proliferation and viability.
source: To evaluate this, we used shRNAs to derive PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells, which displayed normal proliferation and viability (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations mentioned in text and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells harbored reduced H3K27ac at Bim -117.
source: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells also harbored reduced H3K27ac at Bim –117 and reduced Bim mRNA levels, suggesting that PU.1 is responsible for maintaining this enhancer in an active state while, paradoxically, also facilitating TRIM33 recruitment (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F

claim: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells harbored reduced Bim mRNA levels.
source: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells also harbored reduced H3K27ac at Bim –117 and reduced Bim mRNA levels, suggesting that PU.1 is responsible for maintaining this enhancer in an active state while, paradoxically, also facilitating TRIM33 recruitment (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: PU.1 is responsible for maintaining the Bim -117 enhancer in an active state while also facilitating TRIM33 recruitment.
source: PU.1-deficient B-ALL cells also harbored reduced H3K27ac at Bim –117 and reduced Bim mRNA levels, suggesting that PU.1 is responsible for maintaining this enhancer in an active state while, paradoxically, also facilitating TRIM33 recruitment (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-qPCR and RT-qPCR data showing effects of PU.1 knockdown

claim: A high density of PU.1 underlies the skewed distribution of TRIM33 genomic occupancy observed in B-ALL.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that a high density of PU.1 underlies the skewed distribution of TRIM33 genomic occupancy observed in B-ALL.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including motif analysis and PU.1 knockdown effects

claim: Knockdown of TRIM33 led to an increase in PU.1 occupancy at Bim -117.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of TRIM33 led to an increase in PU.1 occupancy and H3K27 acetylation at Bim –117, suggesting that TRIM33 antagonizes PU.1 binding to DNA and suppresses enhancer activity, consistent with prior findings (Kusy et al., 2011) (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Knockdown of TRIM33 led to an increase in H3K27 acetylation at Bim -117.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of TRIM33 led to an increase in PU.1 occupancy and H3K27 acetylation at Bim –117, suggesting that TRIM33 antagonizes PU.1 binding to DNA and suppresses enhancer activity, consistent with prior findings (Kusy et al., 2011) (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I

claim: TRIM33 antagonizes PU.1 binding to DNA and suppresses enhancer activity.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of TRIM33 led to an increase in PU.1 occupancy and H3K27 acetylation at Bim –117, suggesting that TRIM33 antagonizes PU.1 binding to DNA and suppresses enhancer activity, consistent with prior findings (Kusy et al., 2011) (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-qPCR data showing increased PU.1 and H3K27ac upon TRIM33 knockdown, and supported by citation

claim: Knockdown of PU.1 resulted in a reduced sensitivity of B-ALL cells to the lethal effects of TRIM33 knockdown.
source: Consistent with the functional importance of PU.1 antagonism by TRIM33, we found that knockdown of PU.1 resulted in a reduced sensitivity of B-ALL and 38B9 cells to the lethal effects of TRIM33 knockdown (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3J

claim: Knockdown of PU.1 resulted in a reduced sensitivity of 38B9 cells to the lethal effects of TRIM33 knockdown.
source: Consistent with the functional importance of PU.1 antagonism by TRIM33, we found that knockdown of PU.1 resulted in a reduced sensitivity of B-ALL and 38B9 cells to the lethal effects of TRIM33 knockdown (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Bim encodes a BH3-only domain protein with a well-established pro-apoptotic function.
source: Bim encodes a BH3-only domain protein with a well-established pro-apoptotic function (Willis and Adams, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Bim-deficient B-ALL cells were completely resistant to the apoptotic effects of TRIM33 shRNAs.
source: Notably, Bim-deficient B-ALL cells were completely resistant to the apoptotic effects of TRIM33 shRNAs, indicating that Bim is the critical downstream repression target of TRIM33 to maintain cell viability (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Bim is the critical downstream repression target of TRIM33 to maintain B-ALL cell viability.
source: Notably, Bim-deficient B-ALL cells were completely resistant to the apoptotic effects of TRIM33 shRNAs, indicating that Bim is the critical downstream repression target of TRIM33 to maintain cell viability (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Atp1b3 knockdown did not alter the sensitivity of B-ALL to TRIM33 suppression.
source: In contrast, Atp1b3 knockdown did not alter the sensitivity of B-ALL to TRIM33 suppression (data not shown).
evidence: Mentioned as experimental observation

claim: Three independent B-ALL clones harboring a homozygous deletion of the Bim -117 element did not require TRIM33 for viability.
source: Similar to the effects observed upon Bim knockdown, three independent B-ALL clones harboring a homozygous deletion of the −117 element did not require TRIM33 for viability (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Bim knockdown rendered 38B9 cells resistant to the lethal effects of TRIM33 suppression.
source: Bim knockdown and the deletion of the Bim –117 region also rendered 38B9 cells resistant to the lethal effects of TRIM33 suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Deletion of the Bim -117 region rendered 38B9 cells resistant to the lethal effects of TRIM33 suppression.
source: Bim knockdown and the deletion of the Bim –117 region also rendered 38B9 cells resistant to the lethal effects of TRIM33 suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: A single genomic binding site at the Bim locus accounts for the entire TRIM33 requirement in preventing B-ALL apoptosis.
source: This indicates that a single genomic binding site at the Bim locus accounts for the entire TRIM33 requirement in preventing B-ALL apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from CRISPR deletion and rescue experiments

claim: Knockdown of TRIM33 in AML does not result in apoptosis.
source: While both B lymphoid and myeloid leukemia cells harbor PU.1 and TRIM33 at the Bim –117 region, it is important to note that knockdown of TRIM33 in AML does not result in apoptosis or Bim upregulation (Figure 1D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Knockdown of TRIM33 in AML does not result in Bim upregulation.
source: While both B lymphoid and myeloid leukemia cells harbor PU.1 and TRIM33 at the Bim –117 region, it is important to note that knockdown of TRIM33 in AML does not result in apoptosis or Bim upregulation (Figure 1D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: AML cells possess a large cluster of active enhancers located 66 kb upstream of Bim, which is not observed in B-ALL.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of H3K27ac revealed that AML cells possess a large cluster of active enhancers located 66 kb upstream of Bim, which is not observed in B-ALL (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The level of H3K27ac at the AML-specific enhancer cluster at -66 kb is much greater than that observed at the -117 region.
source: Importantly, the level of H3K27ac at this AML-specific enhancer cluster is much greater than that observed at the −117 region.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data comparison

claim: The AML-specific enhancers at the -66 kb region might be the dominant regulatory elements at the Bim locus in AML.
source: This leads us to speculate that the AML-specific enhancers at the −66 kb region might be the dominant regulatory elements at the Bim locus in this cell type.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of ChIP-seq data

claim: The overall strength of AML-specific enhancers may diminish the functional significance of the -117 element, thereby rendering TRIM33 dispensable for AML survival.
source: The overall strength of these enhancers in AML may diminish the functional significance of the −117 element, thereby rendering TRIM33 dispensable for AML survival.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: The role of TRIM33 as a negative regulator of enhancer activity is reminiscent of LSD1.
source: The role of TRIM33 as a negative regulator of enhancer activity is reminiscent of LSD1, a histone demethylase that has been shown previously to suppress active enhancers during embryonic stem (ES) cell differentiation (Whyte et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison with published literature on LSD1

claim: LSD1 suppresses thousands of enhancers in ES cells.
source: However, a key distinction we make here is that LSD1 suppresses thousands of enhancers in ES cells, while TRIM33 preferentially accumulates at a small number of regulatory elements in the B-ALL genome.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The unusual enhancer selectivity of TRIM33 in B-ALL is traced to the density of PU.1.
source: We trace this unusual enhancer selectivity of TRIM33 in B-ALL to the density of PU.1, a TF which has been shown previously to associate with TRIM33 (Kusy et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citation

claim: The binding interaction between TRIM33 and PU.1 is likely to be cooperative on motif-rich DNA elements.
source: This binding interaction is likely to be cooperative on motif-rich DNA elements, which would account for the biased accumulation of TRIM33 at enhancers harboring an exceptional PU.1 density.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: Other transcription factors such as TCF3/E2A are also likely to recruit TRIM33.
source: Our ChIP-seq analysis of TRIM33 in myeloid, B lymphoid, and T lymphoid leukemias suggests that other TFs are also likely to recruit TRIM33, such as TCF3/E2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq and motif analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: TRIM33 is the first example of a mammalian transcriptional regulator that performs an essential function through a single genomic binding site.
source: To our knowledge, TRIM33 is the first example of a mammalian transcriptional regulator that performs an essential function through a single genomic binding site.
evidence: Based on comprehensive experimental characterization and comparison with existing knowledge

claim: The selective occupancy of TRIM33 within the active enhancer landscape may account for the minimal phenotypes observed in TRIM33-deficient mice.
source: The selective occupancy of TRIM33 within the active enhancer landscape may account for the minimal phenotypes observed in TRIM33-deficient mice.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: BRD4 is essential for the maintenance of many cancer types and for the homeostasis of several normal tissues.
source: This is in contrast to the effects of suppressing BRD4, a more general cofactor that is essential for the maintenance of many cancer types and for the homeostasis of several normal tissues (Bolden et al., 2014; Shi and Vakoc, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The localization of TRIM33 to one lineage-specific enhancer upstream of Bim renders B-ALL cells hypersensitive to loss of TRIM33.
source: Remarkably, it is the localization of TRIM33 to one lineage-specific enhancer upstream of Bim that renders B-ALL cells hypersensitive to loss of TRIM33.
evidence: Inferred from CRISPR deletion and rescue experiments

claim: The similar sensitivity of normal and transformed B cells to TRIM33 inhibition implies that the regulatory mechanisms defined in B cell leukemia are likely to have evolved to control normal B cell development.
source: The similar sensitivity of normal and transformed B cells to TRIM33 inhibition implies that the regulatory mechanisms defined here in B cell leukemia are likely to have evolved to control normal B cell development.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of transgenic mouse and B-ALL cell data

claim: Bim is upregulated as a means to eliminate auto-reactive B cells and to prevent autoimmune disease.
source: Interestingly, Bim is upregulated as a means to eliminate auto-reactive B cells and to prevent autoimmune disease, suggesting a rationale for precise modulation of enhancer activity at the Bim locus by TRIM33 to regulate adaptive immunity (Bouillet et al., 1999; Enders et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A reversible depletion of normal B cells is a well-tolerated side effect of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab.
source: In humans, a reversible depletion of normal B cells is a well-tolerated side effect of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab, which is an efficacious therapy in mature B cell neoplasms and in autoimmune disease (Coiffier et al., 2002; Edwards et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published clinical literature

claim: Rituximab is an efficacious therapy in mature B cell neoplasms and in autoimmune disease.

evidence: Supported by citations to published clinical literature

claim: TRIM33 is a promising therapeutic target.
source: Hence, our findings also implicate TRIM33 as a promising therapeutic target, since one of the major phenotypic abnormalities in mice experiencing systemic TRIM33 inhibition is a selective and reversible B lymphocyte deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations in transgenic mice and comparison with rituximab

claim: Bromodomain modules such as BRD4 have proven to be amenable to direct chemical inhibition.
source: Targeting of TRIM33 is particularly attractive since other bromodomain modules (e.g., BRD4) have proven to be amenable to direct chemical inhibition (Prinjha et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A modest expansion of myeloid cells is observed upon short durations of TRIM33 suppression in vivo.
source: However, we observe a modest expansion of myeloid cells upon short durations of TRIM33 suppression in vivo and Trim33−/− mice have been shown to develop chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Aucagne et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from transgenic mice

source: However, we observe a modest expansion of myeloid cells upon short durations of TRIM33 suppression in vivo and Trim33−/− mice have been shown to develop chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Aucagne et al., 2011).

source: Nonetheless, our findings justify consideration of TRIM33-inhibition as a therapeutic approach in B cell neoplasms, which would be expected to unleash an apoptosis-promoting enhancer element.
